title: The account as the unit of isolation, and why there is never just one

videos.script: An AWS account sounds like a login. It is not. It is a box with walls. {{box}} Inside the box are the users, the machines, the limits on how many of each you may have, and one bill. {{five}} Nothing in one box can see into another, unless somebody opens a door on purpose. {{walls}} This lesson shows those walls in your lab. First you read an account number out of the name of a resource. {{arn}} Then you make a second account, and look around from inside it. It has its own network, with the same addresses as the first. It sees none of the first account's users, and none of its topics. {{second}} One thing does cross the walls, and that is the name of a bucket. Take a name in one account, and no other account in the world can have it. {{bucket}} Then comes the reason any of this matters. A company that runs everything in one account shares its mistakes, its limits and its bill. {{one}} So companies split. Production goes in one account and testing in another. Security and logs get accounts of their own. {{split}} The next three lessons arrange those accounts into a tree. This one is about why the tree has more than one leaf. {{end}}
